summary: Describes how to use HDLC framing for PPP packets, marking where each packet starts and ends on a serial link. It was replaced by RFC 1662.

plainLanguage.summary: Words sent down a wire need spaces between them. HDLC framing puts clear markers around each PPP packet.

questions: how ppp frames packets on serial links
subtitle: Framing PPP packets for transmission over serial links.

tldr.problem: The Point-to-Point Protocol needs a way to mark where each packet begins and ends when sending data across serial links, and to handle transparent transmission of control characters.
tldr.mechanism: HDLC framing wraps each PPP packet in flags (0x7e bytes) and adds a 16-bit checksum. When the link type requires it, an escape mechanism prevents data from accidentally looking like frame boundaries.
tldr.outcome: PPP packets can be reliably transmitted across asynchronous, bit-synchronous, and octet-synchronous serial links with clear frame boundaries and error detection. This RFC was later superseded by RFC 1662.

today: RFC 1549 defined the initial standard for PPP HDLC framing. It was a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 1662.

sections.title: Introduction and Frame Basics
sections.content:
PPP is a standard protocol for sending different types of data over point-to-point links. This RFC specifies how to frame PPP packets using HDLC (High-level Data Link Control), a method of marking packet boundaries on serial lines. HDLC framing works on asynchronous links (like RS-232 serial ports), bit-synchronous links (where data arrives bit-by-bit in sync), and octet-synchronous links (where data arrives byte-by-byte in sync).

The challenge is that the link must transparently carry any byte sequence as data, even bytes that are used for framing. HDLC solves this by using an escape mechanism: when data contains special bytes, they are replaced with an escape sequence before transmission, then restored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet gets wrapped with a special marker so the other end knows where it starts and stops. Special data bytes are hidden so the link does not accidentally think they are markers.

sections.title: The HDLC Frame Structure
sections.content:
Every PPP HDLC frame follows the same structure:

The frame begins and ends with a Flag Sequence (0x7e, or 01111110 in binary). Between the flags sits the packet data, structured as: Address (always 0xff, the all-stations address), Control (always 0x03), the PPP protocol field, the packet information, optional padding, and finally a Frame Check Sequence (FCS) that is a 16-bit checksum for error detection.

The Frame Check Sequence is calculated over all the packet data (Address, Control, Protocol, Information and Padding fields) but not the flags or the FCS itself. The same polynomial is used as in HDLC standards and common CRC implementations.

Two consecutive flags with nothing between them represent an empty frame, which is ignored and not treated as an error.
sections.plainLanguage: A frame is like an envelope: a marker at the start, your address and message inside, a number that catches mistakes, and a marker at the end.

sections.title: Transmission on Different Link Types
sections.content:
Asynchronous HDLC (like an RS-232 serial link) transmits one octet at a time with start and stop bits. An octet-stuffing escape mechanism prevents data from containing a frame flag (0x7e) or escape character (0x7d). When the transmitter finds these bytes in the frame, it replaces them with the escape character followed by the byte with bit 6 inverted. The receiver detects the escape and restores the original byte. Characters below 0x20 (control characters) can also be escaped to prevent devices from intercepting them.

Bit-synchronous HDLC works on synchronous links where bits arrive continuously. Instead of octet stuffing, it uses bit stuffing: after every five consecutive 1 bits in the frame, a 0 bit is inserted. The receiver removes any 0 bit that follows five consecutive 1 bits. This ensures the flag sequence (01111110) never appears accidentally in the data. Idle time between frames is filled with flag sequences.

Octet-synchronous HDLC (like SONET) transmits continuous octets without bit stuffing but uses the same octet-stuffing mechanism as asynchronous links. No special control characters are escaped by default, only the flag and escape octets themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Different links need different tricks to avoid mixing up data with frame markers. Slow links escape special bytes, fast links insert and remove bits, and very fast links escape only the marker and escape characters.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 1549 was a Draft Standard specification for PPP HDLC framing. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1662, which updated and refined the framing procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: This was an earlier version of the rules. A newer RFC came along and replaced it.
